title: CPI with Stalls: the Performance Equation GATE Actually Marks
unit: Instruction Pipelining: Hazards, Stalls and Fixes
quickIdea: A real pipeline is compared with CPI = ideal CPI + (stall rate x stall penalty) summed over the hazard classes, and the speed-up is the ratio of execution times - which is the ratio of CPIs only when both designs run at the same clock.
remember: Execution time = CPI x instruction count / frequency (Sarangi equation 10.2). Every speed-up question is a ratio of two of these.
CPI = CPI_ideal + sum over hazard classes of (fraction of instructions x stall cycles each). Ideal CPI is 1 for a scalar pipeline that issues one instruction per cycle.
Speed-up = (CPI_old x T_old) / (CPI_new x T_new). The clock ratio matters, so a 2.5 GHz to 2 GHz redesign must be computed with times, not with CPIs alone.
Stall cycles are added, never averaged: 20 percent stalling 2 and 20 percent stalling 3 is 0.2 x 2 + 0.2 x 3 = 1.0 cycle per instruction, not 2.5.
Only the fraction of instructions that actually stalls pays; a hazard that applies to all instructions needs no fraction.

example.prompt: A non-pipelined processor runs at 2.5 GHz and takes 5 cycles per instruction. It is rebuilt as a 5-stage pipeline that can run only at 2 GHz. In a program, 30 percent of instructions are memory references and 5 percent of those stall 50 cycles on a cache miss; 10 percent are branches and 50 percent of those stall 2 cycles. What is the speed-up?
example.work: Non-pipelined: 5 cycles at 2.5 GHz, so 5 x 0.4 = 2 ns per instruction. Pipelined CPI = 1 + (0.3 x 0.05 x 50) + (0.1 x 0.5 x 2) = 1 + 0.75 + 0.1 = 1.85 cycles, at 2 GHz that is 1.85 x 0.5 = 0.925 ns per instruction. Speed-up = 2 / 0.925 = 2.162.
example.answer: 2.16, the accepted answer of GATE CSE 2020 Q.43. Dividing the CPIs, 5/1.85 = 2.70, would be wrong because the clocks differ.

gateAngle: This is the highest-yield card in the topic. GATE CSE 2020 Q.43 gives stalls of two kinds and two clock rates; GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.58 gives stalls of two kinds at one clock rate and expects 3.0; GATE CSE 2022 Q.61 gives a predictor accuracy instead of a stall count and expects 1.43.

variations.label: PREDICTED VARIATION
variations.question: In the 2020 Q.43 program, what would the speed-up be if the cache-miss stall were 100 cycles instead of 50, everything else unchanged?
variations.why: It isolates the term that dominates the answer and shows how little the branch term matters.
variations.answer: CPI = 1 + 0.3 x 0.05 x 100 + 0.1 = 1 + 1.5 + 0.1 = 2.6; time 2.6 x 0.5 = 1.3 ns; speed-up 2/1.3 = 1.54. Doubling the miss penalty cut the speed-up from 2.16 to 1.54, because 1.5 of the 2.6 cycles are now memory stalls.

variations.label: CONCEPTUAL PRACTICE QUESTION
variations.question: Why must the ideal CPI of 1 be added before the stall terms, and not after the speed-up is computed?
variations.why: It is the single most common arithmetic error in this question family.
variations.answer: Because the pipeline still spends one cycle on every instruction that does not stall. A program where 20 percent stall 2 and 20 percent stall 3 has CPI 1 + 0.4 + 0.6 = 2, not 1.0; using 1.0 as the pipelined CPI doubles the apparent speed-up.

trap.what: Taking the ratio of CPIs when the two designs run at different frequencies.
trap.why: Execution time is CPI divided by frequency, so the frequency enters as well. Ignoring it silently assumes the rebuild was free.
trap.counterexample: 2020 Q.43: CPI ratio 5/1.85 = 2.70 against the true 2.16, because the pipelined machine lost 20 percent of its clock rate.

check.question: A 5-stage pipeline has ideal CPI 1. Twenty percent of instructions stall 2 cycles for data hazards and 20 percent stall 3 cycles for control hazards, at the same clock as the non-pipelined machine whose CPI is 6. What is the speed-up?
check.explanation: This is GATE CSE 2024 Set 2 Q.58 in words; the fractions are multiplied by the stall each class causes and added to the base cycle.

visual.title: Pipelining and Hazards
covers: CPI = 1 + sum of (fraction x stalls), checked against simulation
speedup = (CPI_non x T_non) / (CPI_pipe x T_pipe); the CPI ratio alone is wrong when the clock changes
